summary: Event finding is where the stack is furthest behind Swiss, and the shortfall is measurable rather than a matter of taste. Every timed event inherits two systematic biases from astronomy-engine that Swiss does not have: an Espenak–Meeus Delta-T of 75.4 s in mid-2026 against the observed ~69 s (so Moon events, lunar returns and Moon ingresses land 5–7 s early against both Swiss and JPL Horizons), and a ~1.5" Sun longitude error that the Sun's slow motion amplifies into solar-return and Sun-ingress instants 37–39 s late against Horizons where Swiss is within 1.2 s (0.1–0.24° on the returned chart's ASC/MC). The committed sky data carries a convention defect: build-sky.mjs takes lunations from astronomy-engine's SearchMoonPhase, which uses an aberration-free Sun, so sky.json new/full moons are 40 s late against Horizons, Swiss and the site's own monthly transits files; outer-planet station instants in the same file are 22–37 minutes off Horizons yet published to the millisecond. The crossing solver is a fixed-step sign-change scan with no derivative information: a real 1990 birth constructed so that natal Saturn sits 0.002° (7") below Saturn's 2019 station longitude loses two of its three first-return passes silently in both the site and the package, and yearScan loses grazing Jupiter pairs at dips of 0.005° for two of five grid phases, while the code comment asserts the 5-day step is safe. The package and the site ship two different copies of that solver with different semantics (exact lower endpoint included vs excluded; a hard 10,000-sample throw vs no budget), so SDK users and the site disagree on identical inputs. The transit-window scanner's 0.10/0.15/0.20° budgets are 25–100× the measured slow-planet residual and mark 14% of windows membership-uncertain and 3% exact-uncertain in a ten-chart sample; at a residual-derived 0.003° budget none would be. The things that matter most: fix the time scale (leap-second exact TT−UTC since 1972), put DE-backed or full-series Sun/Moon under the searches, and replace the fixed-step scan with the alpha's derivative-enclosure search so completeness becomes a certified verdict — the one capability Swiss has never offered and the only place this dimension can exceed it.

findings.title: sky.json lunations use an aberration-free Sun: 40 s late vs Horizons, Swiss and the site's own transits files
findings.claim: scripts/build-sky.mjs computes new/full moons with astronomy-engine's SearchMoonPhase, whose MoonPhase → PairLongitude calls GeoVector(body, time, false) (no aberration) for both bodies; the Sun's ~20" annual aberration therefore shifts every lunation instant by ~+40 s relative to the apparent-longitude convention used by the site's charts, by scripts/build-transits.mjs (which bisects bodyLongitude apparent longitudes), by Swiss and by JPL Horizons. Two committed data files disagree by ~40 s for the same physical event and the public sky API publishes the wrong one at millisecond precision.
findings.evidence: node_modules/astronomy-engine/esm/astronomy.js:4247-4256 (PairLongitude uses GeoVector(..., false)) and :4623 (MoonPhase); scripts/build-sky.mjs:199-207 (SearchMoonPhase). Measurement s9: all 124 committed sky.json lunations vs Swiss bisection of apparent Moon−Sun elongation: median |Δ| 32.5 s, p95 40.2 s, max 42.7 s, signed mean +32.8 s (sky later) — out/s9-sky-vs-swiss.json. Internal cross-check: transits-2026-01..11.json lunations minus sky.json for the same 124 events: mean −39.5 s, max 46.3 s (inline python in this audit, reproducible with the two committed files). Horizons arbiter (QUANTITIES 31, apparent, DE441) for the 2027-01-07 new moon: Horizons 20:24:23.225Z, sky.json 20:25:05.910Z (+42.7 s), Swiss 20:24:23.230Z (0.0 s) — out/horizons-arbiter.json, horizons/{sun,moon}-newmoon-2027-01-07.txt. src/lib/sky-api/build.ts:23 joins the two sources with a 6-hour tolerance, so the disagreement is absorbed rather than fixed; src/pages/developers/index.astro:36 advertises /api/v1/moon-phases instants.
findings.reproduction: cd <audit>/production-event-search && <swisslab>/venv/bin/python s9-sky-vs-swiss.py (Swiss part, 5 s); python3 horizons/fetch.py sun-newmoon-2027-01-07 moon-newmoon-2027-01-07 && <swisslab>/venv/bin/python horizons/parse.py (cached responses). Or diff the 'at' of any lunation in src/data/sky.json against the same lunation in src/data/transits-2026-MM.json.
findings.impact: The site's own lunation times are inconsistent with each other and with every reference by 40 s; Swiss users never see this. It also means the homepage/moon-phase/API instants are not the apparent-Sun convention the methodology page implies.
findings.fix: In build-sky.mjs replace SearchMoonPhase with the same apparent-longitude bisection build-transits.mjs uses (bodyLongitude('Moon') − bodyLongitude('Sun') through @zodiacs/engine/internal), regenerate sky.json, add a drift test asserting sky.json and transits-YYYY-MM.json lunations agree to < 2 s, and tighten LUNATION_JOIN_TOLERANCE_MS to minutes.

findings.title: Solar-return and Sun-ingress instants run 37–39 s late against JPL Horizons; Swiss is within 1.2 s
findings.claim: solarReturnInstant and the Sun ingress builder find the correct root of the engine's Sun longitude, but that longitude is ~1.3–1.8" behind DE441 in mid-2026 and the Sun moves only 0.04"/s, so the instant is amplified to ~38 s late; the returned solar-return chart's angles move 0.09–0.24° as a result. The methodology page says solar returns are 'accurate to the same standard as every other chart', which hides the ×24 s-per-arcsecond amplification.
findings.evidence: Swiss matched-target comparison (same natal Sun longitude fed to swe.solcross_ut) over 12 births 1950–2002, returns in 2026: engine − Swiss median +28.1 s, max +40.0 s; natal-derived (Swiss natal Sun) median 16.8 s, max 38.0 s — out/s5b-swiss-returns.json. Sun ingresses 2026–2029 from src/data/ingresses.json vs swe.solcross_ut: n=41, median 9.8 s, p95 28.9 s, max 38.6 s — out/s9-sky-vs-swiss.json. Horizons arbiter (apparent ecliptic longitude, 1-minute table, linear interpolation): solar return C9 (target 101.30535°) Horizons 2026-07-03T04:56:08.417Z, engine +38.8 s, Swiss −1.2 s; C6 engine +37.4 s, Swiss −1.2 s; Sun 60° ingress 2026-05-21 Horizons 00:36:45.484Z, ingresses.json +37.4 s, Swiss −1.2 s — out/horizons-arbiter.json. Chart impact at the engine instant vs the Horizons instant: ASC shift 0.121° (London), 0.242° (New York), MC 0.146–0.177° — out/s12-solar-return-impact.json. Delta-T explains only part: astronomy-engine TT−UT 75.36 s at 2026-07-01 vs Swiss 68.9 s (out/s12, out/s9), which would make Sun events ~6.5 s EARLY, so the Sun series error is ~1.8" (≈45 s) partly offset by the clock.
findings.reproduction: node --experimental-strip-types s5a-returns-engine.mjs > out/s5a-engine-returns.json; <swisslab>/venv/bin/python s5b-swiss-returns.py; python3 horizons/fetch.py sun-solar-return-C9-2026-07-03b sun-solar-return-C6-2026-07-01 && <swisslab>/venv/bin/python horizons/parse.py; node s12-solar-return-impact.mjs.
findings.impact: Solar return charts (the most-used timed chart) carry a systematic ~0.1–0.25° angle error and ~38 s timestamp error that Swiss does not; Sun ingress instants in the public API inherit the same bias. Exceeding Swiss here requires a Sun to better than ~0.05" (≈1 s) or a DE-backed Sun.
findings.fix: Put a DE440-backed (or full untruncated VSOP87 Earth) Sun under bodyLongitude for the Sun/Earth path used by solar-return.ts, year-scan.ts and build-ingresses.mjs, together with finding 3's clock fix; add a Horizons-anchored regression fixture for two solar-return instants with a 3 s gate; state the amplification (24 s per arcsecond) on the methodology page until then.

findings.title: Delta-T model biases every event instant: Moon events 5–7 s early now and growing
findings.claim: astronomy-engine converts the JS Date (UTC) to TT with the Espenak–Meeus polynomial, giving TT−UT = 75.36 s on 2026-07-01 and 76.30 s on 2028-01-01, while the real TT−UTC has been 69.184 s exactly since 2017 (Swiss reports 68.9 s). Every root the crossing solvers find is therefore shifted in UTC by the difference: lunar returns, Moon ingresses, void-of-course boundaries and Moon aspects are ~6 s early today and the error grows ~0.5 s/year.
findings.evidence: out/s12-solar-return-impact.json: astronomyEngineDeltaT_s {2020: 71.578, 2026-07: 75.356, 2028: 76.298, 2100: 202.652}; out/s9: swissDeltaT_s {2026: 68.9, 2028: 68.8}. Lunar returns, same target, engine − Swiss: all 12 cases negative, median −5.25 s, max −6.75 s (out/s5b). Horizons arbiter lunar return C1 (target 168.003078°): Horizons 2026-09-11T02:42:01.117Z, engine −6.6 s, Swiss −0.1 s (out/horizons-arbiter.json, horizons/moon-lunar-return-C1-2026-09-11.txt). Moon sign ingresses 2026–2028 (src/data/aura-moon-ingresses.json, 481 events) vs swe.mooncross_ut: signed mean −5.87 s, max 10.1 s (out/s9). The residual is the Delta-T gap (≈ −6.5 s) partly offset by the missing −0.7" Moon light-time term (finding 13, ≈ +1.3 s). docs/engine-validation/README.md concedes only the 2100 extrapolation (109.5 s) and RESULTS.md the 2.4 s at 2020; the present-day 6.5 s bias is not recorded.
findings.reproduction: node -e "import('astronomy-engine').then(A=>{const t=A.MakeTime(new Date('2026-07-01T00:00:00Z'));console.log((t.tt-t.ut)*86400)})" from the worktree; compare with <swisslab>/venv/bin/python -c "import swisseph as s;print(s.deltat(s.julday(2026,7,1))*86400)"; then s5b / horizons parse as above.
findings.impact: A uniform time bias on every event Zodiacs publishes; Swiss and Horizons agree to ~0.1 s on the Moon. Fixing this alone brings lunar returns, Moon ingresses and VOC boundaries from ~6 s to <1 s of Horizons — better than the 1.2 s Swiss shows on Sun events.
findings.fix: Before calling astronomy-engine, convert UTC → TT with the exact leap-second table (TT−UTC = 32.184 + TAI−UTC, 37 s since 2017) for 1972-01-01 onward, treat UT1−UTC (|DUT1| < 0.9 s) as the only residual and document it, and use IERS Bulletin A/C extrapolation for the next few years; keep Espenak–Meeus only before 1972. Pass the resulting TT into MakeTime via AstroTime.FromTerrestrialTime. Add a fixture: 2026 Moon ingress vs Horizons within 1.5 s.

findings.title: Fixed-step crossing scan silently drops grazing pass pairs in Saturn returns and yearScan; the code comment claims the 5-day step is safe
findings.claim: findLongitudeCrossingsWith (and the package's findLongitudeCrossings) detect roots only by sign change between fixed samples with no station splitting and no derivative bound. When a body stations within a small dip of the target, the two crossings fall inside one 5-day step and are both lost. returns.ts:37-38 asserts 'The default 5-day step is safe for Saturn … a triple pass spans months, never 5 days', which is false for grazing seasons.
findings.evidence: Real-ephemeris construction (out/s3-saturn-graze.json, 12.4 s): Saturn's 2019-04-30T00:48Z retrograde station at 290.51794°; births in Feb 1990 with natal Saturn = station − dip. dip 0.003° (pair 2.7 days apart): saturnReturns and package saturnReturn both report 3 first-return passes (2019-04-28, 05-01, 12-24), matching a 0.25-day reference. dip 0.002° (7.2", pair 2.21 days): both report ONE pass (2019-12-24 only); the 0.25-day reference still finds 3 (2019-04-28T11:25, 05-01T14:15, 12-24T10:04); total crossings 7 → 5, no error, no flag. Saturn curvature at that station −1.64e-3 °/day², so the blind band at a 5-day step is 0.0103° (37"); order-of-magnitude chance per station-bearing season ≈ 6e-5 of natal longitudes. yearScan (Jupiter conjunction to natal Sun, out/s3b-yearscan-phase.json): at dips ≤0.005° (18") the pair is dropped for 2 of 5 grid phases, at 0.001° for 4 of 5; Jupiter blind band 0.0205°. Synthetic mid-cell parabola: pair 4.47 days apart, step 5 → 0 found, step 1 → 2 (out/s3b). docs/platform/evidence/precision-2026-09-20/search/RESULTS.md §5 already records the same mechanism on Uranus (0.002° dip: 5-day scan 0 found); this adds the Saturn-return and yearScan product paths and the false comment.
findings.reproduction: cd <audit>/production-event-search && node --experimental-strip-types s3-saturn-graze.mjs; node --experimental-strip-types s3b-yearscan-phase.mjs (lib/ holds byte-copies of src/lib/engine/*.ts with import specifiers made node-resolvable; node_modules is a symlink to the worktree's).
findings.impact: Rare (≈1 in 10^4 seasons) but silent and unflagged: a user gets one return date where there are three. Swiss offers no guarantee either, so this is parity-at-best; the alpha's derivative-enclosure search is the only route to a certified count.
findings.fix: Short term: in returns.ts/year-scan.ts split the scan at stations exactly as transit-scan-core.ts:231-268 does, or scan at ≤1 day for Jupiter/Saturn (cost ×5, still <1 s), and rewrite the comment to state the blind band. Medium term: back findLongitudeCrossingsWith with the alpha's interval search (examples/precision-alpha/src/core/validated-search.mjs searchGeometricLongitude pattern: exclusion + monotone cells from Lipschitz bounds) and return typed verdicts so an unresolved cell is reported, never dropped.

findings.title: Two crossing solvers ship with different semantics: package includes an exact lower endpoint and throws on a 10,000-sample budget; the site's copy does neither
findings.claim: The site does not use @zodiacs/engine's findLongitudeCrossings; src/lib/engine/longitude-crossings.ts is a separate implementation. They differ observably: (a) an exact root at `from` is returned by the package and excluded by the site; (b) the package throws RangeError once ceil((to−from)/step)+1 or the running sample count exceeds 10,000 (a Moon scan at the 0.25-day step over ~2000+ days), the site has no budget; (c) the package's pendingExact logic drops an exact-zero sample not confirmed by a later sign change, the site emits it immediately. package-integration.test.ts pins versions, not solver parity, and docs/engine-validation/README.md says 'the site runs the same package'.
findings.evidence: out/s2-crossings.json: Sun target = bodyLongitude('Sun', 2026-03-01T00:00Z), window [03-01, 03-03], step 1 → package ['2026-03-01T00:00:00.000Z'], site [] (siteSameInputs.lowerEndpointExact). budget: package Moon 0° over 2100/2400/2600 days at step 0.25 → 'Crossing search exceeds the 10,000-sample budget.' each time; Saturn 1900–2100 at step 5 → same throw; site Moon 2600 days → 95 crossings, no budget. Code: node_modules/@zodiacs/engine/dist/index.js:56-112 (MAX_CROSSING_SAMPLES, pendingExact) vs src/lib/engine/longitude-crossings.ts:23-70. Test coverage of exact endpoints exists only for the site copy (longitude-crossings.test.ts:19-31).
findings.impact: SDK consumers reproducing a site result get a different crossing list or an exception on inputs the site accepts; an SDK transit scanner at the Moon step cannot cover more than ~5.5 years. Swiss has one implementation; a stack claiming to exceed it cannot ship two that disagree.
findings.fix: Make the site import the package solver (or vice-versa) and delete the copy; decide the interval convention ((from, to] per the site tests) and encode it in the package; replace the hard throw with a documented budget parameter and a typed 'refused' result; add a parity test running both on the s2 cases.

findings.title: Transit-window budgets are 25–100× the measured residual and mark 14% of windows uncertain that Swiss would state plainly
findings.claim: transit-window-core.ts fixes angular budgets of 0.10° (planets), 0.15° (angles), 0.20° (Moon) (line 265) and labels a window membership-uncertain or exact-uncertain when a turning point or threshold lies inside that allowance. The measured engine-vs-Swiss slow-planet residual is 3–15" (0.001–0.004°), so the labels are dominated by budget headroom, not by any measured error; users receive 'uncertain' verdicts a Swiss user would never see, and the Uranus D contract stays failed for the same reason.
findings.evidence: out/s6-window-uncertainty.json (12.4 s): ten real charts (1955–2010 births, Placidus, 40.7N) scanned 2026-01-01..2027-12-31 with default options → 641 windows: membershipStatus uncertain 88 (13.7%), exactTopologyStatus uncertain 21 (3.3%), peak.kind 'uncertain' 21. Same charts with angularBudgetDegrees 0.01° → 6 and 2; 0.003° → 0 and 0; 0.001° → 0 and 0; exactPassesTotal 550 in every run (no pass appears or disappears). Measured residuals: RESULTS.md §2 core−Swiss Uranus max 3.45" (0.00096°), Neptune median 11.5" (docs/engine-validation/README.md); RESULTS.md ladder: Uranus D certifies 2 passes at ε ≤ 0.044°. Code: src/lib/engine/transit-window-core.ts:265,280,294-297.
findings.impact: Decisiveness is a capability: Swiss-based software gives exact-pass counts; this product hedges 1 window in 7 on a budget it never measured. The residuals show the hedging is unnecessary at ~10× margin.
findings.fix: Replace the fixed budgets with per-body budgets derived from committed measurements (e.g., 3× the per-body p95 of docs/platform/evidence/swiss-benchmark plus the natal term), record the derivation in docs/engine-validation/transit-windows/README.md, re-run the A–I fixtures with the new contract version (the frozen v2/v3 failure stays recorded), and when a DE-backed backend lands, drop to ε≈0.001° as RESULTS.md §6 already demonstrates.

findings.title: Outer-planet station instants in sky.json are 20–40 minutes off JPL Horizons and published to the millisecond with no uncertainty
findings.claim: build-sky.mjs locates stations by the sign change of a ±6 h finite-difference speed and bisects 16 times (1.3 s resolution). Station time is ill-conditioned (δt = δv/acceleration), so the engine's ~0.05"/day speed error in Neptune/Pluto becomes tens of minutes; the retrogrades page says 'refined to the hour' and the API (/api/v1/stations, /retrogrades) emits ISO milliseconds without any band.
findings.evidence: out/s9-sky-vs-swiss.json: 92 committed station instants vs Swiss analytic-speed zero (bisected to <0.1 s): median |Δ| 170 s, p95 1396 s, max 2463 s; by planet max/median: Pluto 2463/612 s, Neptune 2186/819 s, Uranus 952/349 s, Saturn 813/225 s, Jupiter 295/134 s, Mercury 338/126 s. Horizons arbiter (hourly apparent longitude, quartic fit): Neptune direct station 2027-12-15 Horizons 09:06:03Z, sky.json 09:42:47Z (+2203.6 s), Swiss 09:06:20Z (+17 s); Pluto retrograde station 2028-05-09 Horizons 08:26:01Z, sky.json 08:48:28Z (+1347 s), Swiss(.se1, DE431) 09:29:31Z (+3811 s) — out/horizons-arbiter.json, horizons/{neptune-station-2027,pluto-station-2028}.txt. Code: scripts/build-sky.mjs:53-77,108-129; src/pages/retrogrades/index.astro:76; src/pages/developers/index.astro:33-34.
findings.reproduction: <swisslab>/venv/bin/python s9-sky-vs-swiss.py; python3 horizons/fetch.py neptune-station-2027 pluto-station-2028 && <swisslab>/venv/bin/python horizons/parse.py.
findings.impact: Neptune stations are 2200 s from the DE441 answer where Swiss is 17 s; the API's millisecond timestamps are precision theatre. For Pluto, Swiss with the .se1 files (DE431) is worse than the engine against DE441 — a DE440/441-backed engine would beat Swiss-as-commonly-installed here.
findings.fix: Publish each station with a level-set time envelope (the instants where |speed| ≤ the body's measured speed residual), display 'about HH:MM ± n min' and put the band in the API schema; move the station search onto a DE440-backed longitude (the prototype in docs/platform/evidence/swiss-benchmark/prototype) whose Neptune agrees with Horizons to seconds; add a Horizons-anchored fixture for one Neptune station with a 60 s gate.

findings.title: Eclipse data omits everything Swiss provides beyond peak and kind: contacts, magnitudes, Saros, geography, local circumstances
findings.claim: scripts/build-eclipses.mjs stores type, kind, peak, sign/lon/degree, obscuration and totality minutes. It uses none of the contact times, penumbral/partial durations, greatest-eclipse latitude/longitude, or SearchLocalSolarEclipse that astronomy-engine already exposes, and cannot produce magnitude, Saros series/member, central-line or observer circumstances that swe.sol_eclipse_when_glob/where/how/when_loc and swe.lun_eclipse_how/when_loc return. Peak times themselves agree with Swiss to 14 s.
findings.evidence: out/s8-eclipses-vs-swiss.json: all 24 committed 2026–2030 eclipses vs Swiss: kind matches 24/24; peak residual median 6.3 s, max 13.7 s; committed totalMinutes exceed Swiss totality by 0.7–1.4 min (59 vs 58.3, 72 vs 71.3, 103 vs 101.9, 55 vs 53.6 — the builder rounds 2·sd_total). Swiss fields available and unused, recorded per event in the artifact: Saros series/member (e.g., 2026-08-12 total: 126/48), C1–C4 and totality contacts, umbral/penumbral magnitude, central lat/lon. astronomy-engine surface unused: LunarEclipseInfo.sd_penum/sd_partial, GlobalSolarEclipseInfo.latitude/longitude/distance, SearchLocalSolarEclipse/NextLocalSolarEclipse (node_modules/astronomy-engine/astronomy.d.ts:2781-3028). Code: scripts/build-eclipses.mjs:66-104.
findings.impact: Peak timing is at parity with Swiss (seconds), but the /eclipses/ page and API cannot answer the questions eclipse users ask Swiss-based tools (visible where, when does it start here, how deep). This is a completeness gap, not an accuracy one.
findings.fix: Extend the builder with astronomy-engine's contact times, sd_* durations and greatest-eclipse coordinates now (0.5 d); add a per-observer route using SearchLocalSolarEclipse (partial begin/end, peak altitude, obscuration); compute Saros from the known series epochs (a table lookup); later derive Besselian elements from the DE-backed ephemeris for path polygons. Fix totalMinutes to (sd_total·2) unrounded or to Swiss-style contact difference.

findings.title: build-transits.mjs daily aspect scan claims 'Daily samples catch every crossing'; near a Mercury station a 74" band is blind
findings.claim: scripts/build-transits.mjs:166-211 scans fast×slow and slow×slow exact aspects at one-day steps with a plain sign-change test and asserts completeness in its comment. Two crossings inside one day around a Mercury/Venus/Mars station cancel and are dropped.
findings.evidence: out/s11-transits-blind.json: Mercury station 2026-02-26T06:47:01Z curvature −0.164 °/day² → blind dip 0.0205° (73.8") for a daily scan, 0.13" for hourly; Venus 18.3"; Mars 6.0". With 40 slow-planet aspect targets the per-Mercury-station chance of a silently dropped pair is ≈4.6e-3 (band 2·dip/360 × 40). Ingresses in the same script already use hourly brackets for exactly this reason (lines 105-107), so the inconsistency is internal.
findings.impact: Roughly one dropped exact Mercury aspect pair per few hundred station months in the horoscope event feed; unflagged.
findings.fix: Scan aspects hourly (12 pairs × 8 targets × 720 samples/month is trivial) or split each fast body's scan at its stations as transit-scan-core.ts does; delete the completeness comment or replace it with the measured blind band.

findings.title: Saturn natalRetrograde uses a ±1-day difference while the chart uses ±6 h; they disagree inside a 40 s window around a station
findings.claim: returns.ts:83-87 (and the package computeSaturnReturns) derives natal direction from bodyLongitude(±1 day)/2, whereas computeBodies uses longitudeSpeed(±0.25 day). Neither is the analytic derivative; the two zero-crossings differ, so a birth at a Saturn station gets 'retrograde' from saturnReturns and 'direct' from its own chart.
findings.evidence: out/s4-natal-speed.json: Saturn longitude maximum 2026-07-26T19:57:40.372Z; ±1-day difference zero at 19:56:57.058Z, ±6-hour zero at 19:57:36.921Z, disagreement window 39.9 s; a birth at 19:57:16.990Z gives chart retrograde=false (speed 3.9e-7 °/day) but saturnReturns.natalRetrograde=true in both the site and the package.
findings.impact: Negligible in frequency (40 s per 4.5 months), but it is one product contradicting itself, and a stationary natal Saturn is exactly the case a careful user checks.
findings.fix: Compute natalRetrograde from the same longitudeSpeed the chart uses, or better from an analytic/central-difference derivative with a declared stationary deadband ('stationary' as a third state, as the eight-case policy's 0.02°/day deadband already implies).

findings.title: Return and year scans compute far outside the declared 1800–2199 range without error or flag
findings.claim: saturnReturns/yearScan scan to birth+92 years with no range check; lunar-return.ts and transit-window-core.ts enforce 1800–2199 but returns.ts, solar-return.ts and year-scan.ts do not, so a 2190 birth is scanned to 2282 and a year-900 birth to 992, past astronomy-engine's validated span and on an extrapolated Delta-T, with results presented like any other.
findings.evidence: out/s4-natal-speed.json tail: birth 2150-01-01 → seasons at 2179/2208/2237, scan ends 2242-01-02, threw=false; birth 2190-06-01 → 2219/2248/2278, scan ends 2282-06-02; birth 0900-01-01 → 929/958/988, threw=false. docs/engine-validation/README.md §1 concedes natalChart bounds nothing; the return scanners are not mentioned.
findings.impact: Users can obtain Saturn-return dates for 2280 with the same presentation as 2030; Swiss refuses outside its file range and says so.
findings.fix: Apply the same 1800–2199 (or the eventual DE-backed pack) range check to returns.ts, solar-return.ts and year-scan.ts, clipping the scan window and setting a 'range-clipped' flag the UI renders.

findings.title: Yearly sky/eclipse/ingress/birthday data have no refresh automation or coverage check
findings.claim: Only build-transits.mjs has a cron (transits-monthly.yml). eclipses.json and sky.json (generated 2026-07-20, horizon 2031-01-01), ingresses.json (2026-07-06; fast planets to 2029-07-01), aura-moon-ingresses.json (2026-07-15, to 2029-01-01) and birthdays.json (NOW_YEAR hard-coded 2026) are manual yearly regenerations with no CI check that the display window is still covered.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows: only transits-monthly.yml references a data builder (cron '41 5 25 * *'); src/data/{eclipses,sky,ingresses,aura-moon-ingresses}.json generatedAt/from/to as listed; scripts/build-birthdays.mjs:28 NOW_YEAR = 2026.
findings.impact: Not an accuracy defect today; a missed yearly run silently empties the eclipse/retrograde pages in 2031 and leaves birthday receipts on 2026.
findings.fix: Add a yearly workflow (or extend transits-monthly.yml) that regenerates and PRs the yearly data each July, plus a site-check assertion that each dataset's `to` exceeds today + 12 months.

findings.title: Lunar-return Moon path lacks the −0.7" light-time term the README concedes; sized at +1.3 s of return time
findings.claim: bodyLongitude('Moon') goes through EclipticGeoMoon (CalcMoon rotated into the true ecliptic of date) and never through GeoVector, so no light-time/planetary-aberration correction is applied. Swiss's apparent-minus-geometric Moon difference is a steady −0.67 to −0.74" across 1850–2140, worth ≈1.3 s of lunar-return time (Moon at 0.51–0.57"/s). The README's 'not identical' concession is thus a 1.3 s effect, an order of magnitude smaller than the Delta-T bias in finding 3.
findings.evidence: out/s5b-swiss-returns.json moonEpochs: swiss_apparent_minus_geometric_arcsec −0.7191 (1850), −0.677 (1950), −0.669 (2020), −0.6736 (2026-09-22), −0.6797 (2140); the term is entirely light-time (swiss_lightTimeOnly_effect equals it; Swiss's FLG_NOABERR for the Moon changes a different ±17" quantity). engine − Swiss apparent Moon: 0.16–4.3" modern, 10.2" (2050), 64.8" (2100), 98.8" (2140). Code: chunk-GBH7JIYF.js moonOfDate → EclipticGeoMoon; astronomy.js:3849-3850 GeoVector returns GeoMoon for the Moon unconditionally.
findings.impact: Small, but a stack aiming past Swiss must apply it: with finding 3 fixed, this becomes the largest remaining Moon-event bias.
findings.fix: Backdate the Moon by its light-time (distance/c ≈ 1.28 s) before CalcMoon, or take the Moon from the DE-backed reducer that already applies light-time and aberration (examples/precision-alpha/src/core/reduce.mjs), and record the change in docs/engine-validation/swiss-lunar-return/README.md.

findings.title: Void-of-course: definition, precision and coverage stated; matches the modern 'last exact Ptolemaic aspect' convention
findings.claim: void-of-course.ts implements the void as the interval from the Moon's last exact conjunction/sextile/square/trine/opposition to any of Sun, Mercury–Pluto (default) or Sun–Saturn (option) until the next sign ingress, with no orb, no nodes/asteroids/angles/parallels and no Lilly-style 'applying within orb' rule; ingresses use a 6-hour scan with 24 bisections (1.3 ms), aspects a 3-hour scan with 26 bisections. The relative Moon−planet motion is monotonic (Moon ≥11.8°/day vs Mercury ≤2.2°/day) so the 3-hour scan cannot miss an aspect; the page text matches the code.
findings.evidence: src/lib/engine/void-of-course.ts:15-33,74-141,148-169; src/pages/void-of-course-moon/index.astro:66,74,243-249; tests void-of-course.test.ts (7 cases incl. a 30-minute brute-force sweep and a cross-check against aura-moon-ingresses to 1 s). Moon ingress instants vs Swiss (out/s9): n=481, median 5.9 s, max 10.1 s, all early — the Delta-T bias of finding 3, not a solver defect. Mainstream references: Astrodienst/Solar Fire default to the ten-planet exact-aspect rule; traditionalists (Lilly) use an orb-based applying rule, which is not offered.
findings.reproduction: Read the cited lines; run the s9 script for the ingress residuals.
findings.impact: At parity with mainstream software; Swiss has no VOC function. With finding 3 fixed the boundaries would be within ~1 s of Horizons.
findings.fix: Optional: add the Lilly/orb variant and an 'applying to the next-sign aspect' flag as options; publish the definition string with each API window.

findings.title: Progressions: tropical-year day-for-a-year (365.2422 mean solar days per civil day), planets only, no alternative rates
findings.claim: progressions.ts maps elapsed time in units of 365.2422 × 86400 s onto civil days from birth (PROGRESSION_DAYS_PER_YEAR = 365.2422) and computes bodies only; progressed angles (Naibod 59'08"/yr, solar-arc MC, mean quotidian) and the Q2 'true solar arc' day-for-a-year variant are not offered. The methodology page states the convention accurately. Solar Fire's default and most Swiss-based apps use the same 365.2422 mapping; 365.25 and Q2 are user options there.
findings.evidence: src/lib/engine/progressions.ts:11,20-23; src/pages/methodology/index.astro:162-165; progressions.test.ts covers the mapping against a constructed JPL fixture (1 ms gate) and the 12–15°/yr progressed Moon rate.
findings.impact: Correct and honest but thinner than Swiss-based software; no accuracy issue.
findings.fix: Add year-length option (365.25 Julian) and progressed angles via Naibod and solar-arc MC with the convention stamped in the receipt; the solar-arc variant needs a progressed-Sun search which the crossing solver already supports.

findings.title: Half-day transit-window sampling is sound for the slow bodies: 12-hour motion ≤0.121° and stations ≥117 days apart
findings.claim: transit-window-core's 12-hour grid cannot lose a 3° orb entry/exit (a body would have to traverse 6° in 12 h) and cannot hide a crossing pair, because a pair requires a turning point inside the cell and turns are bracketed by the grid's slope-sign test with at least 117 days between them. The Moon and fast bodies never enter this scanner (transitBodies restricted to Jupiter–Pluto); transit-scan-core scans Sun/Mercury/Venus/Mars by default and the Moon when the TransitSearch UI selects it (0.25-day step, station-split irrelevant), the calendar API scans the defaults over −31/+183 days.
findings.evidence: out/s7-slow-bounds.json (37.8 s, 292,194 half-day samples per body 1800–2200): max |Δλ| per 12 h Jupiter 0.12126° (1892-03-21), Saturn 0.0652°, Uranus 0.0316°, Neptune 0.0190°, Pluto 0.0203°; minimum station spacing Jupiter 117.5 d, Saturn 133.5 d, Uranus 149 d, Neptune 156 d, Pluto 156 d. Code: transit-window-core.ts:57-61,108-131,176-194; transit-scan-core.ts:95-106 (STEP_DAYS incl. Moon 0.25), TransitSearch.worker.ts:41 includeMoon, TransitSearch.tsx:46-50 (1/5/10-year spans), api/calendar/transits.ts:10-11.
findings.impact: No sampling defect in the window scanner; the remaining weakness there is the budget policy of finding 6.
findings.fix: Record these bounds in the transit-windows README as the sampling argument (they are currently asserted, not shown).

findings.title: Path to exceed Swiss: certified completeness from the alpha's derivative-enclosure search behind every production crossing
findings.claim: Swiss Ephemeris offers no completeness guarantee for any event function (solcross/mooncross return the next root by iteration; users find stations by speed sign and everything else by their own scans). The alpha already proves completeness for geometric longitude crossings in a fixed J2000 frame (searchGeometricLongitude: exclusion and monotone cells from Chebyshev-coefficient Lipschitz bounds) and has of-date/aberration/retarded ladders with interval enclosures; the deflection layer failed its usefulness rule and the partition is partial. Production uses none of it.
findings.evidence: examples/precision-alpha/src/core/validated-search.mjs:1-55,372 (proof sketch and entry point); RESULTS.md §3-6 (typed verdicts crossing/no-crossing/stationary-touch/multiple-crossings/boundary-event/unresolved-interval; Uranus D certified at ε=0.001° on DE440s); this audit's findings 4 and 5 show what the fixed-step scan drops. Swiss API surface enumerated from pyswisseph 2.10.03: solcross(_ut), mooncross(_ut), mooncross_node(_ut), helio_cross(_ut), sol_eclipse_when_glob/loc/where/how, lun_eclipse_when/when_loc/how, lun_occult_when_glob/loc/where, rise_trans(_true_hor), heliacal_ut/heliacal_pheno_ut, nod_aps(_ut), pheno(_ut) — none carries a completeness contract.
findings.reproduction: cd examples/precision-alpha && npm test (tier A, no data) for the proven analytic cases; RESULTS.md run-all.sh for the Uranus D certification.
findings.impact: This is the one dimension where 'more advanced than Swiss' is achievable with existing repository code: a return, transit or ingress result that says 'these are all the crossings, proven' or 'this cell is unresolved' instead of a list that may be short.
findings.fix: (1) Compile a DE440s pack (tools/compiler) and ship a fixed-frame geometric certification alongside each production crossing list as a count check; (2) extend the interval enclosures through the of-date frame and aberration (both ladders exist) to certify apparent tropical crossings, declaring the empirical curvature bound where the proof does not reach; (3) route findLongitudeCrossingsWith/saturnReturns/yearScan/transit-scan-core through it with typed verdicts surfaced in the UI; (4) leave deflection out until it passes its own rule.
